name: Department of Survey and Land Information (DOSLI)
story: DOSLI operated from 1987 to 1996 during a substantial part of the digital land-information transition. Its work included cadastral and topographic data, survey and mapping. The later division into LINZ and Terralink separated regulatory and public functions from commercial services, with data, systems and staff continuing across the change.

DOSLI was established in April 1987 when Lands and Survey was restructured. It provided government civil and military surveying, mapping and land-information services; land development and conservation management went to other organisations. In 1995 the Land Titles Office moved from the Department of Justice to DOSLI. On 1 July 1996 DOSLI’s functions were divided between LINZ and Terralink.

A contemporary account makes the cadastral programme more specific. Allan Wilson, writing from DOSLI’s Cadastral Services in April 1990, described the Digital Cadastral Database under development and its intended role as a common geographic framework. The stated benefits extended beyond departmental mapping to public services, land-management decisions and private-sector analysis. That was an ambition for a maintained national dataset and its users, rather than simply the purchase of GIS software.

The resulting data also had a long afterlife. LINZ’s legacy-system documentation traces DCDB geometry back to cadastral record maps digitised from the mid-1980s and records its later conversion into Landonline. District maintenance continued into 2000–02. DOSLI’s closure in 1996 and the replacement of its digital cadastral system were separate events.

photoGallery.title: DOSLI in photographs
photoGallery.intro: Nathan Heazlewood supplied seven photographs from the same period and a later LINZ newsletter clipping. One print is labelled “Cartographic Directorate 1995”. The clipping, dated May 1999, names the people in its own inset team photograph; it does not identify the people in the separate prints.
photoGallery.credit: Seven photographs and a Landlink clipping provided by Nathan Heazlewood.
